title: Global zero-excitation state preparation through subsystem cooling
abstract: Preparing interacting quantum systems in low-energy or ground states is a fundamental task in quantum simulation and quantum information processing. In realistic settings, dissipation and active cooling can typically be engineered only on a limited subset of the system. We study the dissipative dynamics of excitation-number conserving quantum systems governed by a GKLS master equation with local jump operators acting on a subset of qubits. We establish sufficient conditions under which such localized dissipation drives the full system to a unique globally attractive zero-excitation state. In particular, we prove that if the Hamiltonian generates excitation transfer described by a graph for which the dissipative subsystem forms a zero forcing set, then the zero-excitation state is the unique globally attractive stationary state. When this state coincides with a ground state of the Hamiltonian, the same mechanism realizes ground-state cooling. Our results provide a graph-theoretic criterion for global state preparation from localized dissipation, which we illustrate using a nearest-neighbor Heisenberg spin chain. For this model, a reduction to the single-excitation sector further yields a scaling estimate with the length of the chain which indicates efficient cooling.
summary: This paper develops a graph-theoretic criterion to determine when cooling a small part of a large, interacting quantum system can force the entire system into its lowest energy (zero-excitation) state. By analyzing the dynamics under a GKLS master equation, the authors show that the structure of the system's interactions, specifically the 'zero-forcing set' property, dictates the possibility of global state preparation. This offers a powerful tool for designing quantum simulators with limited access to cooling mechanisms.
main_problem: The paper investigates the conditions under which localized dissipation acting on a subset of an interacting quantum system can drive the entire system to a unique, globally attractive zero-excitation state.
main_result: Sufficient conditions are established, linking global state preparation to the graph-theoretic property that the dissipative subsystem forms a zero-forcing set of the excitation-transfer graph.
method: The analysis uses the GKLS master equation framework, combining rigorous mathematical proofs with graph theory (zero-forcing sets) to derive structural criteria for convergence.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as coupled qubits governed by a Hamiltonian $H$ and dynamics described by a GKLS master equation with local jump operators. The study is illustrated using a nearest-neighbor Heisenberg spin chain.
key_observables: Global zero-excitation state, the zero-forcing property of the excitation-transfer graph, and the reduced single-excitation gap ($\Delta_{	ext{red}}(n)$).
important_parameters: The scaling estimate for the reduced gap is found to be $\Delta_{	ext{red}}(n) \propto n^{-3}$, indicating efficient cooling.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to excitation-number conserving qubit systems and assumes localized, lowering-type dissipation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates localized cooling on a subset of qubits. Figure 3 shows the system-size scaling of the single-excitation gap estimate, demonstrating $n^{-3}$ decay.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical problem (localized cooling) to establishing mathematical conditions (Proposition II.1) using the GKLS equation, connecting these conditions to graph theory (zero-forcing sets), and finally providing quantitative estimates using a specific model (Heisenberg chain) to confirm the scaling.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, general graph-theoretic criterion for achieving global quantum control (ground state preparation) using only local environmental coupling, which is highly relevant for designing realistic quantum simulators.
